sentences.text: Elasmosaurus is a genus of elasmosaurid plesiosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous in what is now the United States, and the only recognized species is Elasmosaurus platyurus.
This marine reptile possessed a neck that was approximately 7.1 meters long.
Its neck contained 72 vertebrae, a count higher than any other plesiosaur except Albertonectes.
The animal had four sacral vertebrae, which is the typical number for elasmosaurids.
Edward Drinker Cope distinguished Elasmosaurus from Cimoliasaurus by its longer neck with compressed vertebrae versus a shorter neck with square, depressed vertebrae.
Elasmosaurus had approximately three pectoral vertebrae, a trait shared with many other elasmosaurids.
The long and low axis of the vertebral centrum in Elasmosaurus differs from many other plesiosaurs, which have centers shorter in length than in height, or nearly equal in dimensions.
A replica of the Elasmosaurus skeleton at the Fort Wallace Museum measures approximately 12.8 meters in length.
A polished stone found in a tail vertebra of the holotype is hypothesized to be a gastrolith.

Fossil evidence shows elasmosaurids were preyed upon, including a humerus with bite marks from the shark Cretoxyrhina and a crushed Eromangasaurus skull with tooth marks from the pliosaur Kronosaurus.
While long-necked Jurassic plesiosaurs from England were already well known, Elasmosaurus was the first known from the Cretaceous period.

The genus Elasmosaurus was named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1868 after the first specimen was discovered in early 1867 by army surgeon Theophilus Hunt Turner and scout William Comstock near Fort Wallace, Kansas.
The holotype specimen of Elasmosaurus was not redescribed in detail until 2005 by German paleontologist Sven Sachs.
The function of Elasmosaurus's long neck is unknown, though it may have been used for feeding.
Elasmosaurids likely ate small fish and marine invertebrates, possibly using gastroliths to aid digestion.
In 1869, Cope found scales and teeth from six fish species beneath the vertebrae of the Elasmosaurus holotype.
Elasmosaurids may have hunted in the pelagic zone by retracting their necks to strike or using side-swipe motions to stun prey with their teeth.
Cope envisioned the snake-like head of Elasmosaurus being raised high, arched like a swan before striking fish, or stretched while resting on the water.
A study found elasmosaurid necks could move 75–177 degrees ventrally, 87–155 degrees dorsally, and 94–176 degrees laterally.
Elasmosaurids were fully adapted to ocean life with streamlined bodies and long paddles indicating they were active swimmers.
Elasmosaurus was a slow swimmer that likely ambushed schools of fish.
In 1906, Williston considered the vertebrae of E. intermedius mutilated and found no distinct differences from E. platyurus.
Welles moved the species Elasmosaurus snowii to the genus Styxosaurus in 1943.
Carpenter placed Elasmosaurus morgani in its own genus, Libonectes, in 1997.
Elasmosaurus fossils date to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period, and the animal lived in North America between 80.6 and 77 million years ago.
At its largest, the Western Interior Seaway stretched from the Rockies to the Appalachians, approximately 1000 km wide.
Edward Drinker Cope initially believed the original Elasmosaurus material represented two different animals, referring to one as Discosaurus carinatus in a 1868 letter.
In 2007, paleontologists Leslie Noè and Marcela Gómez-Pérez doubted that additional fossils found near the original site belonged to the type specimen or to Elasmosaurus.
The validity of several Russian species previously assigned to Elasmosaurus has been questioned by researchers.
